screens.title: Configuration Management with Red Hat Satellite and Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore how Red Hat Satellite and Ansible work together to deliver consistent, auditable configuration for RHEL infrastructure. You will learn the two integration pillars: Satellite as a dynamic inventory source and Satellite as a management point for Ansible roles and playbooks. We’ll show concrete examples: installing the foreman. foreman plugin on an Ansible control node to query Satellite, importing an Ansible role from Git, assigning that role to a host group, and running it using Satellite’s UI or hammer CLI. Along the way we explain common failures you’ll see in the field, like SSH connectivity issues or missing Python on clients, and how to verify job reports in Satellite. This matters because architects need automated, repeatable configuration that follows lifecycle and compliance rules from provisioning through updates. By the end of the lesson you’ll understand how dynamic inventory avoids stale hosts lists, how Satellite stores and triggers roles, and where to look when execution fails. Keep in mind: use least-privilege service accounts and test new roles in lower environments before broad rollouts.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Overview
Configuration Management with Satellite + Ansible
Integrate Satellite’s lifecycle controls with Ansible’s declarative playbooks to enforce host state.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
This chapter walks through the practical setup and workflows you need as an architect: enabling the foreman-proxy Ansible plugin, configuring Satellite as a dynamic inventory via the foreman.foreman collection, importing roles from Git, assigning them to host groups, running plays from the UI or hammer CLI, and inspecting job reports to troubleshoot failures. You’ll see worked command examples and a hands-on activity to import an Nginx role and apply it to a host group.
Why this matters
Automation reduces drift and ensures compliance from provisioning to runtime. Satellite + Ansible ties content and configuration together.
Practical outcome
You’ll be able to use Satellite as an inventory source and trigger roles so new hosts are configured automatically.

Hosts, groups, parameters
Ansible Roles

Execution
UI, CLI, Capsules

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map directly to hands-on capabilities you need when integrating Satellite with Ansible. First, you will explain how Satellite and the Ansible Automation Platform integrate so you can justify architecture decisions. Second, you'll configure Satellite to act as a dynamic inventory source for an external Ansible control node using the foreman. foreman inventory plugin. Third, you will import and assign Ansible roles to host groups and hosts inside Satellite, understanding role precedence and parameter overrides. Fourth, you will trigger Ansible playbooks or roles from the Satellite UI or the hammer CLI and interpret job reports to troubleshoot problems. Each objective ties a skill to a purpose: reliable automation, reduced drift, auditable runs, and faster recovery from failures. As you progress, verify each objective by importing a simple Nginx role and confirming it installs on a test host. That verification habit turns knowledge into repeatable practice.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Lab & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on lab practice and common troubleshooting tasks you'll face. You will create or use a simple Ansible role, push it to a Git repository or make it available locally, and import it into Satellite. Then you will attach that role to a Host Group and confirm that new or existing hosts receive it during provisioning or via a triggered run. You will also learn to read Satellite job reports for output, failure codes, and tracebacks. Troubleshooting covers typical causes: blocked SSH, missing Python on clients, misconfigured role syntax, and permission issues for the service account that Satellite uses to run Ansible. The lab reinforces safer practices: use least-privilege service accounts, protect SSH keys, and test roles in lower environments. Successful completion means you can import a role, assign it, run it, and verify the managed host reflects the expected configuration, such as an Nginx service running with a specific index page.

screens.title: Dynamic Inventory with Satellite
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic inventory is the practice of letting Ansible query an authoritative system for the current list of managed hosts and their attributes rather than relying on a static hosts file. In the Satellite integration, Satellite acts as that authoritative source. This means when you register a host with Satellite, it becomes immediately available to Ansible runs that use the foreman. foreman plugin. A concrete example: instead of maintaining a manually edited hosts file that may miss new VMs, you install the foreman. foreman collection on your control node and write an inventory. yml that points to your Satellite URL and A P I credentials. When you run ansible-inventory against that inventory file, Ansible asks Satellite for hosts, groups, and parameters, and you receive an up-to-date JSON inventory. A common misconception is that dynamic means slower; in practice, querying Satellite is fast and far safer than a stale static file. Another contrast to remember is that dynamic inventory centralizes source-of-truth, which reduces human error during provisioning. Key checks include ensuring the Satellite user has A P I access and validate_certs is set appropriately. Takeaway: using Satellite for inventory removes drift and simplifies targeting for playbooks.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Dynamic inventory lets Ansible query Satellite for current hosts, groups, and parameters, eliminating static hosts files.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Dynamic Inventory
What is dynamic inventory?
Satellite supplies a live list of managed hosts and parameters to Ansible via a plugin so your control node always targets the correct hosts.
  • Eliminates the need for a manually maintained hosts file.
  • Automatically reflects provisioning, decommissioning, and group changes.
  • Exposes host parameters that roles can consume as variables.
Concrete Example
Install the foreman.foreman collection and create an inventory.yml that points to Satellite. Running an inventory list returns current hosts.
Key Takeaway

Dynamic inventory centralizes host discovery to prevent targeting errors and reduce operational drift.

Inventory Setup — Visual Steps
The following code snippet is the minimal inventory.yml you use on your Ansible control node to talk to Satellite.
plugin: foreman.foreman.foreman
url: https://satellite.example.com
username: ansible_user  # A Satellite user with API access
password: your_secure_password
validate_certs: true
# Optional: host_filters:
#  - content_view = "RHEL8_Base_CV"
#  - hostgroup = "Web Servers"
Run verification commands to confirm hosts are returned and reachable.
ansible-galaxy collection install foreman.foreman
ansible-inventory -i inventory.yml --list
ansible -i inventory.yml all -m ping
Misconception: Dynamic inventory removes access controls. It simply centralizes discovery; you still need proper API credentials and network access.

screens.title: Enabling Ansible Integration in Satellite
screens.narratorSegment: To enable Satellite’s Ansible integration you need the foreman-proxy-plugin-ansible installed on the Satellite Server or on a Capsule that will execute jobs. The satellite-installer commonly enables this by default, but you should confirm installation and placement for your architecture. The practical reason for this separation is execution locality: running Ansible from a Capsule near the managed hosts reduces network hops and improves performance. A common setup flow is to confirm the plugin’s package is installed, ensure the Capsule has network access and A P I connectivity back to Satellite, and validate that the Capsule can SSH to clients. A frequent misconception is that Ansible execution always originates from Satellite; in larger deployments you typically use Capsules to distribute execution. Example commands are deployment-specific, but verification steps include listing configured Capsules in Satellite and testing an ad-hoc run against a small host group. Key takeaway: install the plugin where execution will logically occur and validate SSH, A P I, and permissions before scaling runs. This avoids surprises during broad rollouts. Enabling Ansible Integration in Satellite means install foreman-proxy-plugin-ansible on the satellite or capsule that will logically execute jobs; capsules reduce latency and central load.. In practical terms, install and verify the foreman ansible plugin and capsule placement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Enable Integration
Enable the plugin
Confirm foreman-proxy-plugin-ansible is installed on the Satellite Server or Capsule that will run jobs. Decide execution locality based on where managed hosts live.
Decide Capsule vs Satellite
Use a Capsule near hosts for large deployments to reduce latency and central load.
Validate
Ensure Capsule/Satellite can reach managed hosts over SSH and has API connectivity back to Satellite if required.
Verification and Tests
Use small, targeted runs to confirm configuration before broad execution. Example: pick a single host and run a simple role or ping module through Satellite.
# Example verification steps (conceptual)
# 1. Confirm package: foreman-proxy-plugin-ansible is present on capsule or satellite
# 2. Check capsule can SSH to client and that API traffic is allowed
# 3. Trigger a small run from UI and inspect Monitor → Jobs for status
Common misconception: Installing the plugin is sufficient. You must also ensure network, credentials, and permissions are correct for execution to succeed.

screens.title: Using the foreman.foreman Inventory Plugin
screens.narratorSegment: The foreman. foreman collection is the Ansible-side connector that allows your control node to query Satellite for hosts and metadata. Start by installing the collection on your Ansible control node using ansible-galaxy. Then create a simple inventory. yml that points to your Satellite server and provides A P I credentials. This inventory file tells Ansible to call the foreman A P I and return groups, hosts, and host parameters. A concrete example: after installing the collection, creating inventory. yml with your Satellite URL and a service account, you can run ansible-inventory -i inventory. yml --list to see a JSON representation of the current inventory. Next, run ansible -i inventory. yml all -m ping to verify connectivity to all returned hosts. A common mistake is leaving validate_certs set to true without configuring certificates in lab environments; in production you should validate certificates, but for an isolated lab you may need false temporarily. Finally, be careful with credentials — use a least-privilege account with A P I access. The core idea: this plugin removes the need for manual hosts management and keeps your control node in sync with Satellite.

keyIdea.title: Plugin Use
keyIdea.text: Install foreman.foreman on the control node and configure inventory.yml to let Ansible query Satellite for live inventory.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › foreman.foreman Plugin
Install the collection
On your Ansible control node install the collection so the plugin is available to inventory lookups.
ansible-galaxy collection install foreman.foreman
Create inventory.yml as shown and secure the credentials with vault or environment variables in production.
# inventory.yml
plugin: foreman.foreman.foreman
url: https://satellite.example.com
username: ansible_user  # A Satellite user with API access
password: your_secure_password
validate_certs: true
# Optional: host_filters:
#  - content_view = "RHEL8_Base_CV"
#  - hostgroup = "Web Servers"
Verify inventory and connectivity
Use ansible-inventory to list hosts and then run a simple ping module across the inventory to confirm Ansible can reach returned hosts.
ansible-inventory -i inventory.yml --list
ansible -i inventory.yml all -m ping
Contrast: A static hosts file can become out-of-date when hosts are provisioned or retired. Using Satellite keeps inventory accurate and auditable.

screens.title: Importing Ansible Roles into Satellite
screens.narratorSegment: Satellite can import Ansible roles so you manage configuration code alongside content and lifecycle. The common and recommended workflow is to store roles in a Git repository and import them from Configure → Ansible → Roles using the repository URL. Satellite will clone the repo and expose the roles for assignment. If Git integration isn't possible in a lab, a local path import or copying the role into an expected directory can work, but production should favor Git for traceability. A concrete example is preparing a simple Nginx role, initializing a Git repo locally, pushing it to a remote, and providing that URL to Satellite’s import function. Once imported, roles appear in Satellite’s roles list and can be added to host groups. A typical misconception is that roles in Satellite become packages; they remain Ansible artifacts that Satellite references and executes. Key checks include validating role syntax before import and ensuring the Satellite service account has read access to the repository. The outcome is central role management and a single place to assign configuration to host groups. Importing Ansible Roles into Satellite means import roles from a git repo for traceable, centralized management; local path imports are possible for labs but less ideal for production.. In practical terms, from git repository or local path to role available in satellite. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Import Roles
Recommended: Git import
Push your role to a Git repository and import it via Satellite UI: Configure → Ansible → Roles → Import from Git.
Before importing, validate role structure and syntax to avoid runtime errors after assignment.
Lab Note
If you cannot use a remote Git repo in the lab, copy the role to a path on Satellite and discover it with hammer or UI discovery methods.
Example role structure (conceptual)
nginx_role/
  tasks/
    main.yml
  templates/
    index.html.j2
  defaults/
  meta/
After import, roles are selectable when editing Host Groups or individual hosts under the Ansible Roles tab.
Misconception: Importing a role alone will not apply it automatically until it is assigned to a host group or run manually.

screens.title: Assigning Roles to Host Groups and Hosts
screens.narratorSegment: After roles are available in Satellite, you assign them to Host Groups or individual hosts. This mapping lets any host in a host group inherit configuration automatically, which is essential for scaling. When you edit a Host Group and add roles under the Ansible Roles tab, those roles apply to all hosts that belong to the group. You can also add or override variables at the host group or host level; Satellite exposes host parameters with a clear precedence: organization, location, host group, then individual host. A concrete example: define apache_port in a host group for web servers and reference it in your role as {{ apache_port }}. If one host needs a different port, set the parameter at the individual host level and it will override the host group value. A common mistake is assuming role variables are immutable once assigned; in Satellite you can override parameters at multiple levels, which is powerful but requires disciplined naming and change control. Key takeaway: use host groups for broad configuration and host-level overrides sparingly to maintain predictability. Assigning Roles to Host Groups and Hosts means assign roles to host groups for scale; host parameters follow a precedence chain allowing safe overrides when necessary.. In practical terms, how satellite maps roles to groups, and how parameter precedence works. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Assign roles to host groups for scale; host parameters follow a precedence chain allowing safe overrides when necessary.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Assign Roles
Assign roles to host groups
Open Configure → Host Groups, edit the group, and add roles under Ansible Roles. Any host in that group inherits the role application when runs are triggered.
  • Host Group assignment scales configuration across many systems.
  • Roles can also be added at an individual host level for exceptions.
  • Parameters can be defined at multiple levels to customize behavior.
Parameter precedence
Satellite parameters around provisioning and Ansible follow clear precedence: organization → location → host group → host. Use this to plan defaults and safe overrides.
Example
Set apache_port at the host group level for all web servers, then override on a single host if needed. The host-level parameter wins.
Tip: Avoid per-host overrides when possible to reduce configuration sprawl and simplify auditing.

screens.title: Triggering Ansible Runs from Satellite
screens.narratorSegment: Satellite provides two common ways to execute Ansible roles: directly from the UI and via the hammer CLI. From the UI you can select one or more content hosts or a host group and click Run Ansible Roles; Satellite will execute the assigned roles and provide a job report. For scripted or automated workflows, use hammer job-invocation create with the feature ansible_roles and a job-template such as Run Ansible Roles. The chapter includes an example hammer command that passes a search-query and a parameters argument to specify the roles to run. When running roles, expect Satellite to orchestrate connections over SSH and return detailed logs. A common misconception is that UI runs are for demos only; in many environments UI runs are used for one-off maintenance while CLI runs are used in automated pipelines. Always validate execution with a quick test run on a small set of hosts and inspect Monitor → Jobs for output. The key operational habit is to check job reports immediately after a run so you can detect SSH or role errors while context is fresh.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Run Roles
Run via Satellite UI
Select Hosts → Content Hosts, choose targets, and click Run Ansible Roles to execute assigned roles. Inspect Monitor → Jobs for the report.
When to use UI
One-off maintenance, exploratory runs, or small-scale verification.
Run via hammer CLI
Use hammer for scripted invocations and automation pipelines. The following example triggers a job template and passes an ansible role parameter to a specific host via search query.
hammer job-invocation create \
--feature ansible_roles \
--job-template "Run Ansible Roles" \
--search-query "name = myclient.example.com" \
--parameters "ansible_roles=apache_webserver_role" \
--organization "MyOrg"
Note: Use search queries to target groups or named hosts and parameterize role selection as needed.

screens.title: Ansible Roles and Playbooks in Satellite
screens.narratorSegment: An Ansible role is a structured collection of tasks, templates, variables, files, and metadata that automates configuration for a specific component or service. A playbook is a YAML file that orchestrates plays, each targeting a group of hosts and calling tasks or roles. Satellite stores roles and can host simple playbooks to help apply consistent configuration across hosts. When Satellite runs roles, it references the role content and executes tasks over SSH on the managed hosts. An important distinction to keep in mind: Satellite manages the lifecycle and distribution of roles, but the execution logic remains Ansible’s. A common error is to expect Satellite to translate roles into RPM packages or content views; roles remain Ansible artifacts applied at runtime. Use roles to encapsulate idempotent configuration: installing packages, managing services, and templating files. For example, an nginx role will install the nginx package, enable the service, and deploy a template for index. html. Key takeaway: treat roles as versioned, testable modules of configuration that Satellite can assign and run for scalable, repeatable state management. Ansible Roles and Playbooks in Satellite means roles are reusable modules; playbooks orchestrate roles across target hosts. satellite stores and triggers roles but execution is ansible-driven.. In practical terms, what satellite stores and how it executes role-based configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Roles & Playbooks
What Satellite stores
Satellite will clone or reference role content imported from Git or local paths and surface them in the UI for assignment to host groups and hosts.
Example Role Behavior
An nginx role should install the package, enable and start the service, and deploy a templated index page using provided variables.
Role sample task (conceptual)
---
- name: Install Nginx
  ansible.builtin.dnf:
    name: nginx
    state: present

- name: Start and enable Nginx service
  ansible.builtin.systemd:
    name: nginx
    state: started
    enabled: true

- name: Copy Nginx default index page
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: index.html.j2
    dest: /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
    mode: '0644'
Remember to validate role syntax and test in a lab environment before broad assignment.

screens.title: Common Failures and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When Ansible runs triggered by Satellite fail, the most frequent root causes are SSH connectivity, missing Python on the client, role syntax errors, and permission or network issues between Satellite/Capsule and the targets. Start troubleshooting by inspecting the job report in Monitor → Jobs to get the raw Ansible output. If you see connection errors, verify SSH is running on the client, firewall rules allow access, and credentials (keys or password) are correct. If tasks fail with Python import errors, ensure a supported Python interpreter is installed on the client so Ansible modules can execute. For syntax errors, validate your roles locally with ansible-lint or a dry run before import. A common misconception is to blame Satellite first; often the problem is network or client-side configuration. Use a step-by-step approach: check job output, validate connectivity, confirm interpreter presence, and review role logs. The key operational discipline is to reproduce the failure against a single host for rapid iteration before attempting cluster-wide remediation. Common Failures and Troubleshooting means inspect job output, verify ssh connectivity, ensure python exists on clients, and validate role syntax to isolate ansible execution failures.. In practical terms, why ansible runs from satellite fail and how to diagnose them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.6 › Troubleshooting
Common failure modes
  • SSH connectivity blocked by firewall or wrong credentials.
  • Missing Python interpreter on the managed host prevents module execution.
  • Syntax or role errors introduced before import.
  • Insufficient permissions for the Satellite user or network segmentation blocking Capsules.
Diagnosis steps
  1. Open the job report in Monitor → Jobs to read raw Ansible logs.
  2. Verify SSH to the client from the execution point; check keys and firewall rules.
  3. Confirm Python exists on the client and is in PATH.
  4. Run role syntax checks locally and re-import if needed.
Misconception: Job failures always mean role issues. Begin with connectivity and client checks first; they are most common.

screens.title: Security and Operational Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Security and change control are critical when Satellite runs Ansible across many hosts. Use dedicated, least-privilege service accounts for Ansible A P I access and limit their abilities to only what is necessary. Protect SSH keys used for remote execution: store them in a secure vault or use centralized key management, and rotate them regularly. Treat Ansible roles as code: version them in Git, run continuous validation tests, and deploy first to lower environments before production. Implement change management for role parameter changes so overrides are reviewed and audited. A common operational mistake is to allow unrestricted host-level parameter overrides; restrict these and prefer host group defaults. Additionally, log and retain job reports for auditing and post-change verification. Finally, document execution locality decisions — why a Capsule runs jobs for a set of hosts — so future operators understand the topology. The key insight: secure credentials and disciplined change control are as important as the automation itself. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore how Red Hat Satellite and Ansible work together to deliver consistent, auditable configuration for RHEL infrastructure. You will learn the two integration pillars: Satellite as a dynamic inventory source and Satellite as a management point for Ansible roles and playbooks. We’ll show concrete examples: installing the foreman. foreman plugin on an Ansible control node to query Satellite, importing an Ansible role from Git, assigning that role to a host group, and running it using Satellite’s UI or hammer CLI. Along the way we explain common failures you’ll see in the field, like SSH connectivity issues or missing Python on clients, and how to verify job reports in Satellite. This matters because architects need automated, repeatable configuration that follows lifecycle and compliance rules from provisioning through updates. By the end of the lesson you’ll understand how dynamic inventory avoids stale hosts lists, how Satellite stores and triggers roles, and where to look when execution fails. Keep in mind: use least-privilege service accounts and test new roles in lower environments before broad rollouts.

These objectives map directly to hands-on capabilities you need when integrating Satellite with Ansible. First, you will explain how Satellite and the Ansible Automation Platform integrate so you can justify architecture decisions. Second, you'll configure Satellite to act as a dynamic inventory source for an external Ansible control node using the foreman. foreman inventory plugin. Third, you will import and assign Ansible roles to host groups and hosts inside Satellite, understanding role precedence and parameter overrides. Fourth, you will trigger Ansible playbooks or roles from the Satellite UI or the hammer CLI and interpret job reports to troubleshoot problems. Each objective ties a skill to a purpose: reliable automation, reduced drift, auditable runs, and faster recovery from failures. For example, setting up dynamic inventory removes the need for a fragile, manually maintained hosts file, which is a common cause of deployment mistakes. As you progress, verify each objective by importing a simple Nginx role and confirming it installs on a test host. That verification habit turns knowledge into repeatable practice.

This second objectives slide focuses on lab practice and common troubleshooting tasks you'll face. You will create or use a simple Ansible role, push it to a Git repository or make it available locally, and import it into Satellite. Then you will attach that role to a Host Group and confirm that new or existing hosts receive it during provisioning or via a triggered run. You will also learn to read Satellite job reports for output, failure codes, and tracebacks. Troubleshooting covers typical causes: blocked SSH, missing Python on clients, misconfigured role syntax, and permission issues for the service account that Satellite uses to run Ansible. The lab reinforces safer practices: use least-privilege service accounts, protect SSH keys, and test roles in lower environments. Successful completion means you can import a role, assign it, run it, and verify the managed host reflects the expected configuration, such as an Nginx service running with a specific index page.

Dynamic inventory is the practice of letting Ansible query an authoritative system for the current list of managed hosts and their attributes rather than relying on a static hosts file. In the Satellite integration, Satellite acts as that authoritative source. This means when you register a host with Satellite, it becomes immediately available to Ansible runs that use the foreman. foreman plugin. A concrete example: instead of maintaining a manually edited hosts file that may miss new VMs, you install the foreman. foreman collection on your control node and write an inventory. yml that points to your Satellite URL and A P I credentials. When you run ansible-inventory against that inventory file, Ansible asks Satellite for hosts, groups, and parameters, and you receive an up-to-date JSON inventory. A common misconception is that dynamic means slower; in practice, querying Satellite is fast and far safer than a stale static file. Another contrast to remember is that dynamic inventory centralizes source-of-truth, which reduces human error during provisioning. Key checks include ensuring the Satellite user has A P I access and validate_certs is set appropriately. Takeaway: using Satellite for inventory removes drift and simplifies targeting for playbooks.

To enable Satellite’s Ansible integration you need the foreman-proxy-plugin-ansible installed on the Satellite Server or on a Capsule that will execute jobs. The satellite-installer commonly enables this by default, but you should confirm installation and placement for your architecture. The practical reason for this separation is execution locality: running Ansible from a Capsule near the managed hosts reduces network hops and improves performance. A common setup flow is to confirm the plugin’s package is installed, ensure the Capsule has network access and A P I connectivity back to Satellite, and validate that the Capsule can SSH to clients. A frequent misconception is that Ansible execution always originates from Satellite; in larger deployments you typically use Capsules to distribute execution. Example commands are deployment-specific, but verification steps include listing configured Capsules in Satellite and testing an ad-hoc run against a small host group. Key takeaway: install the plugin where execution will logically occur and validate SSH, A P I, and permissions before scaling runs. This avoids surprises during broad rollouts. Enabling Ansible Integration in Satellite means install foreman-proxy-plugin-ansible on the satellite or capsule that will logically execute jobs; capsules reduce latency and central load.. In practical terms, install and verify the foreman ansible plugin and capsule placement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The foreman. foreman collection is the Ansible-side connector that allows your control node to query Satellite for hosts and metadata. Start by installing the collection on your Ansible control node using ansible-galaxy. Then create a simple inventory. yml that points to your Satellite server and provides A P I credentials. This inventory file tells Ansible to call the foreman A P I and return groups, hosts, and host parameters. A concrete example: after installing the collection, creating inventory. yml with your Satellite URL and a service account, you can run ansible-inventory -i inventory. yml --list to see a JSON representation of the current inventory. Next, run ansible -i inventory. yml all -m ping to verify connectivity to all returned hosts. A common mistake is leaving validate_certs set to true without configuring certificates in lab environments; in production you should validate certificates, but for an isolated lab you may need false temporarily. Finally, be careful with credentials — use a least-privilege account with A P I access. The core idea: this plugin removes the need for manual hosts management and keeps your control node in sync with Satellite.

Satellite can import Ansible roles so you manage configuration code alongside content and lifecycle. The common and recommended workflow is to store roles in a Git repository and import them from Configure → Ansible → Roles using the repository URL. Satellite will clone the repo and expose the roles for assignment. If Git integration isn't possible in a lab, a local path import or copying the role into an expected directory can work, but production should favor Git for traceability. A concrete example is preparing a simple Nginx role, initializing a Git repo locally, pushing it to a remote, and providing that URL to Satellite’s import function. Once imported, roles appear in Satellite’s roles list and can be added to host groups. A typical misconception is that roles in Satellite become packages; they remain Ansible artifacts that Satellite references and executes. Key checks include validating role syntax before import and ensuring the Satellite service account has read access to the repository. The outcome is central role management and a single place to assign configuration to host groups. Importing Ansible Roles into Satellite means import roles from a git repo for traceable, centralized management; local path imports are possible for labs but less ideal for production.. In practical terms, from git repository or local path to role available in satellite. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After roles are available in Satellite, you assign them to Host Groups or individual hosts. This mapping lets any host in a host group inherit configuration automatically, which is essential for scaling. When you edit a Host Group and add roles under the Ansible Roles tab, those roles apply to all hosts that belong to the group. You can also add or override variables at the host group or host level; Satellite exposes host parameters with a clear precedence: organization, location, host group, then individual host. A concrete example: define apache_port in a host group for web servers and reference it in your role as {{ apache_port }}. If one host needs a different port, set the parameter at the individual host level and it will override the host group value. A common mistake is assuming role variables are immutable once assigned; in Satellite you can override parameters at multiple levels, which is powerful but requires disciplined naming and change control. Key takeaway: use host groups for broad configuration and host-level overrides sparingly to maintain predictability. Assigning Roles to Host Groups and Hosts means assign roles to host groups for scale; host parameters follow a precedence chain allowing safe overrides when necessary.. In practical terms, how satellite maps roles to groups, and how parameter precedence works. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Satellite provides two common ways to execute Ansible roles: directly from the UI and via the hammer CLI. From the UI you can select one or more content hosts or a host group and click Run Ansible Roles; Satellite will execute the assigned roles and provide a job report. For scripted or automated workflows, use hammer job-invocation create with the feature ansible_roles and a job-template such as Run Ansible Roles. The chapter includes an example hammer command that passes a search-query and a parameters argument to specify the roles to run. When running roles, expect Satellite to orchestrate connections over SSH and return detailed logs. A common misconception is that UI runs are for demos only; in many environments UI runs are used for one-off maintenance while CLI runs are used in automated pipelines. Always validate execution with a quick test run on a small set of hosts and inspect Monitor → Jobs for output. The key operational habit is to check job reports immediately after a run so you can detect SSH or role errors while context is fresh.

An Ansible role is a structured collection of tasks, templates, variables, files, and metadata that automates configuration for a specific component or service. A playbook is a YAML file that orchestrates plays, each targeting a group of hosts and calling tasks or roles. Satellite stores roles and can host simple playbooks to help apply consistent configuration across hosts. When Satellite runs roles, it references the role content and executes tasks over SSH on the managed hosts. When Ansible runs triggered by Satellite fail, the most frequent root causes are SSH connectivity, missing Python on the client, role syntax errors, and permission or network issues between Satellite/Capsule and the targets. Start troubleshooting by inspecting the job report in Monitor → Jobs to get the raw Ansible output. If you see connection errors, verify SSH is running on the client, firewall rules allow access, and credentials (keys or password) are correct. If tasks fail with Python import errors, ensure a supported Python interpreter is installed on the client so Ansible modules can execute. For syntax errors, validate your roles locally with ansible-lint or a dry run before import. A common misconception is to blame Satellite first; often the problem is network or client-side configuration. Use a step-by-step approach: check job output, validate connectivity, confirm interpreter presence, and review role logs. The key operational discipline is to reproduce the failure against a single host for rapid iteration before attempting cluster-wide remediation. Security and change control are critical when Satellite runs Ansible across many hosts. Use dedicated, least-privilege service accounts for Ansible A P I access and limit their abilities to only what is necessary. Protect SSH keys used for remote execution: store them in a secure vault or use centralized key management, and rotate them regularly. Treat Ansible roles as code: version them in Git, run continuous validation tests, and deploy first to lower environments before production. Implement change management for role parameter changes so overrides are reviewed and audited. A common operational mistake is to allow unrestricted host-level parameter overrides; restrict these and prefer host group defaults. Additionally, log and retain job reports for auditing and post-change verification. Finally, document execution locality decisions — why a Capsule runs jobs for a set of hosts — so future operators understand the topology. The key insight: secure credentials and disciplined change control are as important as the automation itself. A second set of concepts helps you operate the integration reliably. Remote Execution indicates Satellite uses SSH to run Ansible tasks on clients, so verify connectivity and keys. Host Parameters are the editable key-value pairs in Satellite that roles can consume for customization and have a defined precedence chain; use them to avoid hard-coded values.
